L5@P0: April 13, 2026
L6@P0: Back to overweight U.S. stocks
L7@P0: • U.S.-Iran negotiations collapsed for now, but we see talks as evidence of an
L8@P0: economic incentive to end the conflict. We upgrade risk in U.S. and EM stocks.
L9@P0: • A U.S.-Iran ceasefire saw oil prices slide, stocks bounce and bond yields drop.
L10@P0: We could see a partial unwind of those moves after the breakdown in talks.
L11@P0: • We watch U.S. PPI to see if energy-driven cost pressures keep pushing prices
L12@P0: up. We expect modest growth in China as external demand fuels recovery.
L13@P0: We flagged two signposts to dial up risk-taking after the Middle East conflict led us
L14@P0: to reduce risk and turn neutral on U.S. equities a few weeks ago. First: evidence of
L15@P0: actions that could re-open shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Second: signs
L16@P0: that any lingering macro impact is contained. We eye developments on both fronts.
L17@P0: Plus, corporate earnings expectations are up even through the conflict, partly on
L18@P0: the AI theme. We go back to modest risk taking and turn overweight U.S. stocks.

L23@P0: Talks between the U.S. and Iran broke down over the weekend, but we think the fact
L24@P0: that they began in the first place indicates that there are strong economic
L25@P0: incentives for all parties to end the conflict. We saw two signposts that would lead
L26@P0: us to re-up risk after reducing it a few weeks ago. First, tangible evidence of actions
L27@P0: that would reopen flows through the Strait of Hormuz. And second, visibility on the
L28@P0: lingering macro impact being contained. This comes as expectations for corporate
L29@P0: earnings have climbed for both the U.S. and EM for 2026 – even since the conflict
L30@P0: began on Feb. 28. See the chart. We see the AI theme at play in both. Companies in
L31@P0: South Korea and Taiwan – key producers of the hardware needed for AI – are driving
L32@P0: EM earnings upgrades. In the U.S., the forecast 80% boost to semiconductor stock
L33@P0: earnings this year are helping drive upgrades in tech and overall, LSEG data show.

L74@P1: We are eyeing developments on both of these signposts. A breakdown in U.S.-Iran negotiations over the weekend could add
L75@P1: to near-term pressure on risk assets. But both countries agreeing to start talks is concrete evidence of economic incentives to
L76@P1: de-escalate, in our view. China’s role – and U.S. President Donald Trump’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping
L77@P1: in mid-May – is likely factoring into those economic incentives. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz would need to pick back
L78@P1: up for a sustained positive impact on markets. We use our proprietary tracker to monitor traffic through the strait. In terms of
L79@P1: the macro impact, we see it as significant and don’t necessarily expect a return to the environment in place before the conflict
L80@P1: began – but think other drivers can outweigh that impact and go back to moderate risk taking on a tactical horizon.
L81@P1: One of those drivers? Corporate earnings getting revised up, even as equities have pulled back. Tech’s valuation premium has
L82@P1: been eroded, with the 12-month forward valuation of the U.S. IT over other sectors at its lowest level since mid-2020. At the
L83@P1: same time, the tech sector is now seen posting earnings growth of 43% in 2026, up from 26% last year. These bright spots
L84@P1: partly inform our upgrade to U.S. equities. AI earnings exposure also contributes to our modest EM overweight. We are
L85@P1: funding this equity upgrade by reducing our cash-like preference of front-end euro area government bonds, which we took a
L86@P1: few weeks ago after a sharp pricing in of European Central Bank rate hikes early in the conflict.
L87@P1: We will keep emphasizing thematic opportunities accelerated by events in the Middle East – and think those exposures will
L88@P1: benefit no matter the outcome. We saw mega forces creating a world shaped by supply factors such as tariffs and labor
L89@P1: constraints before the conflict began – and think this will persist after it ends. We see geopolitical fragmentation supporting
L90@P1: defense and aerospace, spurring governments to push even harder for energy independence and leading companies to invest
L91@P1: more in supply chain resilience. Along with the AI theme, that will drive demand for infrastructure and power.
L92@P1: Bottom line: We see evidence of economic incentives to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. We turn moderately positive risk and like
L93@P1: U.S. stocks as a relative preference, seeing them holding up better even if absolute performance disappoints. We also turn
L94@P1: overweight EM stocks and still favor thematic opportunities like defense.

L134@P2: Our highest conviction views on six- to 12-month (tactical) and over five-year (strategic) horizons, April 2026
L135@P2: Strategic Reasons
L136@P2: Portfolio construction We favor a scenario-based approach as AI winners and losers emerge. We lean on private
L137@P2: markets and hedge funds for idiosyncratic returns and to anchor portfolios in mega forces.
L138@P2: Infrastructure equity and
L139@P2: private credit
L140@P2: We find infrastructure equity valuations attractive and mega forces underpinning structural
L141@P2: demand. We still like private credit but see dispersion ahead – highlighting the importance of
L142@P2: manager selection.
L143@P2: Beyond market cap
L144@P2: benchmarks
L145@P2: We get granular in public markets. We favor DM government bonds outside the U.S. Within
L146@P2: equities, we favor EM over DM yet get selective in both. In EM, we like India which sits at the
L147@P2: intersection of mega forces. In DM, we like Japan as mild inflation and corporate reforms
L148@P2: brighten the outlook.
L149@P2: Note: Views are from a U.S. dollar perspective, April 2026. This material represents an assessment of the market environment at a specific time and is not intended to be a forecast of future events
L150@P2: or a guarantee of future results. This information should not be relied upon by the reader as research or investment advice regarding any particular funds, strategy or security.
L151@P2: Tracking five mega forces
L152@P2: Mega forces are big, structural changes that affect investing now – and far into the future. They change the longterm growth and inflation outlook and are poised to create big shifts in profitability across economies and
L153@P2: sectors. This creates major opportunities – and risks – for investors. See our web hub for our research.
L154@P2: 1. Demographic divergence: The world is split between aging advanced economies and younger emerging
L155@P2: markets – with different implications.
L156@P2: 2. Digital disruption and artificial intelligence (AI): Technologies are transforming how we live and work.
L157@P2: 3. Geopolitical fragmentation and economic competition: Globalization is being rewired as the world splits
L158@P2: into competing blocs.
L159@P2: 4. Future of finance: A fast-evolving financial architecture is changing how households and companies use
L160@P2: cash, borrow, transact and seek returns.
L161@P2: 5. Transition to a low-carbon economy: The transition is set to spur a massive capital reallocation as energy
L162@P2: systems are rewired.

L166@P2: Tactical Reasons
L167@P2: Favor AI beneficiaries
L168@P2: Markets are increasingly focused on identifying companies exposed to AI disruption. We favor
L169@P2: physical infrastructure and equipment supporting the AI buildout – such as semiconductors,
L170@P2: power and data center assets – that we think we stand to benefit no matter the winners or losers.
L171@P2: Selected international
L172@P2: exposures
L173@P2: We like hard-currency EM debt due to improved economic resilience, disciplined fiscal and
L174@P2: monetary policy and a high ratio of commodities exporters. In Europe, we favor equity sectors
L175@P2: such as infrastructure.
L176@P2: Evolving diversifiers
L177@P2: We suggest looking for a “plan B” portfolio hedge as long-dated U.S. Treasuries no longer
L178@P2: provide portfolio ballast – and to mind potential sentiment shifts. We like gold as a tactical play
L179@P2: with idiosyncratic drivers but don’t see it as a long-term portfolio hedge.

L185@P2: came in higher than expected. The U.S. March CPI showed a surge in energy inflation at the headline level
L186@P2: but limited impact in core inflation. In China, we expect to see signs of modest but steady growth as
L187@P2: external demand – rather than domestic momentum – gradually powers a recovery.

L192@P3: Granular views
L193@P3: Six- to 12-month tactical views on selected assets vs. broad global asset classes by level of conviction, April 2026
L194@P3: Asset View Commentary
L195@P3: Equities
L196@P3: Developed markets
L197@P3: United States We go overweight. Contained damage to global growth from the Mideast conflict and strong
L198@P3: earnings expectations – particularly in tech – keep us risk-on.
L199@P3: Europe We are neutral. Europe’s high exposure to the energy shock from the Mideast conflict makes it
L200@P3: vulnerable to higher inflation and lower growth.
L201@P3: UK We are neutral. Valuations remain attractive relative to the U.S., but we see few near-term
L202@P3: catalysts to trigger a shift.
L203@P3: Japan We are neutral. Japan’s exposure to imported energy may erode strong equity gains powered
L204@P3: by healthy corporate balance sheets and governance reforms.
L205@P3: Emerging markets We go overweight, yet stay selective. We favor Asian countries that manufacture critical AI
L206@P3: components and Latin American energy and commodity exporters.
L207@P3: China
L208@P3: We are neutral. Trade relations with the U.S. have steadied, but property stress and an
L209@P3: aging population still constrain the macro outlook. Relatively resilient activity limits near-term
L210@P3: policy urgency. We like sectors like AI, automation and power generation.
L211@P3: Short U.S. Treasuries We are neutral. Shorter-term bonds are relatively attractive as the market has woken up to
L212@P3: persistent inflation and higher rates.
L213@P3: Long U.S. Treasuries
L214@P3: We are underweight. Yields already faced upward pressure from rising term premia, as investors
L215@P3: demand more compensation for the risk of holding long-term debt. The recent energy price
L216@P3: shock compounds this by aggravating pre-existing inflationary pressures.
L217@P3: Fixed Income
L218@P3: Global inflation-linked
L219@P3: bonds
L220@P3: We are neutral. We think inflation will settle above pre-pandemic levels, but markets may not
L221@P3: price this in the near term as growth cools.
L222@P3: Euro area govt bonds
L223@P3: We go neutral short-term European government bonds. The market has repriced the ECB policy
L224@P3: path more in line with our view. We think increased German bond issuance to finance its fiscal
L225@P3: stimulus package is already largely reflected in the current level of 10-year yields.
L226@P3: UK gilts We are neutral. We expect volatility in gilts over the near-term. Gas powers much of the UK’s
L227@P3: electricity, but storage is limited – making it especially vulnerable to a resurgence in inflation.
L228@P3: Japanese govt bonds We are underweight. Rate hikes, higher global term premium and heavy bond issuance will
L229@P3: likely drive yields up further.
L230@P3: China govt bonds We are neutral. China bonds offer stability and diversification but developed market yields are
L231@P3: higher and investor sentiment shifting towards equities limits upside.
L232@P3: U.S. agency MBS We are overweight. Agency MBS offer higher income than Treasuries with similar risk and may
L233@P3: offer more diversification amid fiscal and inflationary pressures.
L234@P3: Short-term IG credit We are neutral. Corporate strength means spreads are low, but they could widen if issuance
L235@P3: increases.
L236@P3: Long-term IG credit We are underweight. We prefer short-term bonds less exposed to interest rate risk over longterm bonds.
L237@P3: Global high yield We are neutral. High yield offers more attractive carry and shorter duration, but we think
L238@P3: dispersion between higher and weaker issuers will increase.
L239@P3: Asia credit We are neutral. Overall yields are attractive and fundamentals are solid, but spreads are tight.
L240@P3: Emerging hard currency We are overweight. EM hard-currency indexes lean toward Latin American commodity exporters
L241@P3: such as Brazil that stand to benefit as Mideast supply plummets.
L242@P3: Emerging local currency We are neutral. The U.S. dollar has been strengthening as a safe-haven currency in the wake of
L243@P3: the Middle East conflict. This could reverse year-to-date gains driven by a falling USD.
